# Bit-serial modular multiplication — radix-4 fork of neural-horner v8

A ~471K-parameter recurrent cell run in a fixed bit-serial Horner loop, computing (a·b) mod p for primes to 2^2048 and operands to 4096 bits. Fork of Robby Sneiderman's neural-horner v8 (MIT); unmodified v8 is submitted separately as an attributed baseline.

Public benchmark: overall 98.9%, highest tier ≥90% = 10, 129.7 s on a 4090 against a 300 s budget; across 6 seeds, T10 mean 96.3% (min 92%).

## Architecture

One shared p-conditioned cell (bidirectional 3-layer GRU, d_model 96, hidden 128, radix-4 digit and op embeddings, per-bit head) learns s' = (4s + d·x) mod p, d ∈ {0,1,2,3}. A learned op-embedding selects its three uses: reduce a mod p, reduce b mod p, multiply the residues. Radix-4 halves the step count against radix-2 at equal parameter count. Warm-started from v8 with the op-embedding zero-initialised, so at k=1 it reproduces v8 bit-for-bit.

`weights.pt` is a uniform weight-space average (model soup) of an annealed checkpoint and a same-recipe re-anneal; it beat both endpoints on identical problems (one-sided McNemar p = 0.02, n = 1008). `weights_t1.pt` serves primes of bit-length ≤ 3. Width policy: groups of ≥257 bits run at min(2080, pbits+32), 17–256 at pbits, <17 at 32.

Compliance: no controller, the schedule takes no feedback from the model, every arithmetic step including the conditional subtraction comes from the trained cell, and both routing choices key on the prime's bit-length alone — the shape ruled acceptable in the Zulip fixed-loop-encoder thread.

## Findings

**1. A training grid on round bit-lengths has zero tier coverage.** Ours sampled primes only at multiples of 32 bits; tier primes are drawn uniformly and land almost entirely below those boundaries, so states carrying leading zeros had zero training coverage. Grouping by exact bit-length at inference moved the public benchmark from 73.3% to 91.3% with no retraining.

**2. State width is a first-class inference hyperparameter, and its response is not monotonic.** Paired same-problem measurements: 0 leading zeros usable but not optimal deep (effective ε ≈ 2.2e-5); 1 zero is a dead zone (~5% collapse); 31–32 optimal (ε ≈ 1.8e-6, deep errors ~5× fewer — T10 49→9 of 1008, T9 19→5, T8 18→2, McNemar p ≤ 1e-4); 64 a clone of 32 (error sets identical, Jaccard 1.00).

The gain is representational headroom, not training familiarity: primes at exact multiples of 32, trained at field-filling width, are the worst cells at that width in the deepest tier (9 errors of 48 at 2048 bits, 1 of 48 with +32). And +32 ≠ ceil-32 — ceil-32 pushes x·32−1-bit primes, which the generator produces in quantity, into the dead zone. We falsified ceil-32, shelved the family, and lost a week. Chain length is not the mechanism: with N ≈ ⌈abits/k⌉+⌈bbits/k⌉+⌈W/k⌉ the axis moves N by 0.6% while moving ε over 10×.

**3. Small primes are unreachable in any sampling stream.** random_prime-style constructors emit odd values with the top bit set, so p = 2 must be injected explicitly. Our T1 sat at 61%; worse, our own battery could not see p = 2 either, so the hole was first misfiled as a false alarm. The fused single-step universe for p ∈ {2,3,5,7} is 348 transitions — enumerate it rather than sample it.

## What did not work

Continued training failed in three forms. Unanchored tiny-prime fine-tuning cured small primes and ate large-scale precision (T8 −8, T10 −13). L2-SP, which I had proposed in the Zulip thread, has no λ window: λ = 10/30/100 relocates the interference rather than removing it (512-bit cells 166→170→172 while 64/128/256-bit cells fall monotonically). A same-recipe re-anneal paid nothing. The mechanism is measurable: our single-step validation floor is ~8e-6 while effective ε is already 1.8e-6, so both the objective and checkpoint selection sit below the instrument. Coverage and precision are zero-sum at this capacity. Ensembling over widths or across checkpoints failed too, and bf16 was acquitted as a hypothesis.

Method note: below ~2pp, paired same-problem comparison beats cross-seed averaging outright; our cross-seed noise was ±3.4 per cell.

## Limits

The deep-chain ε tail is deferred, not solved (T10 min 92%). Small primes needed a second routed checkpoint because one weight set could not hold both regimes. We cannot explain why 1 leading zero is a dead zone. The remaining structural lever is raising the radix (k=3 cuts N by 33%); we ran out of time.

## Attribution

Derived from neural-horner (github.com/Robby955/neural-horner) by Robby Sneiderman, MIT licensed. The architecture and the compliance framing originate there; the radix-4 fusion, width policy, tiny-prime handling and the negative results are ours. Thanks to the SAIR organizers for the fixed-loop-encoder ruling, and to that thread's participants for the capacity-versus-coverage reports that shaped our diagnosis.
